blocks.text: An air-filled balloon immediately shoots up to the surface when released under the surface of water; the same happens if a piece of wood is released under water. A mug filled with water feels light under water but heavy as soon as we take it out. More than two thousand years ago the Greek scientist Archimedes noticed that an upward force acts on an object kept inside a liquid, so that an apparent loss of weight is observed in the object; this upward force is the upthrust of the liquid.

blocks.title: Archimedes' principle
blocks.text: When an object is totally or partially immersed in a liquid, an upthrust force acts on it equal to the weight of the liquid it displaces.

Consider a solid cylinder of cross-sectional area A and height h immersed in a liquid (Fig. 5.8). Let h1 and h2 be the depths of the top and bottom faces from the surface: h2 - h1 = h ... (5.11). If P1 and P2 are the liquid pressures at depths h1 and h2 and rho the density, P1 = rho g h1 and P2 = rho g h2. The force F1 exerted at the top by the liquid due to P1 and the force F2 at the bottom due to P2 are F1 = P1 A = rho g h1 A and F2 = P2 A = rho g h2 A. F1 and F2 act on opposite faces, so the net force F on the cylinder is their difference, the upthrust of the liquid: F2 - F1 = rho g h2 A - rho g h1 A = rho g A (h2 - h1) ... (5.12), or upthrust = rho g A h, or upthrust = rho g V ... (5.13). Here A h is the volume V of the cylinder, equal to the volume of liquid displaced, so rho g V is the weight of the liquid displaced: an upthrust acts on a body immersed in a liquid equal to the weight of the liquid displaced, which is Archimedes' principle. Archimedes was born about 287 BCE in Syracuse on the island of Sicily and was killed by a Roman soldier after he refused to leave his mathematical work (For Your Information).

blocks.title: Example 5.2
blocks.text: A wooden cube of side 10 cm is dipped completely in water. Calculate the upthrust of water acting on it. Solution: L = 10 cm = 0.1 m; V = L^3 = (0.1 m)^3 = 1 x 10^-3 m^3; rho = 1000 kg m^-3; F = ?. Using Archimedes' principle, upthrust = rho g V = 1000 kg m^-3 x 9.8 m s^-2 x 1 x 10^-3 m^3 = 9.8 N.

An object sinks if its weight is greater than the upthrust acting on it; it floats if its weight is equal to or less than the upthrust. When an object floats in a fluid the upthrust on it equals the weight of the object; a floating object may be partially immersed, and the upthrust always equals the weight of the fluid displaced. This is the principle of floatation: a floating object displaces a fluid having weight equal to the weight of the object. Archimedes' principle applies to liquids as well as gases, and has numerous applications in daily life.

blocks.long_description: The liquid pressure on the bottom face of an immersed cylinder exceeds that on the top face by the density times g times the height, so the net upward force is the weight of the liquid the cylinder displaces, which is Archimedes' principle; a body floats when its weight is no more than this upthrust, and then displaces its own weight of fluid, which explains hot-air balloons, floating wood, ships and submarines. In streamline flow every particle through a point follows the path of those before it and streamlines never cross, whereas above a certain speed the flow becomes turbulent with eddies; an ideal fluid is non-viscous, incompressible and steady. The volume passing a section per second is the area times the speed, and because mass is conserved this product is the same at every section of a pipe, so a narrowing pipe speeds the flow up.

items: Hot-air balloon (Fig. 5.9): hot-air balloons rise and float in mid-air because the density of the hot-air balloon is less than that of the surrounding air; when the buoyant force on the balloon is more than its weight it starts to rise, which is done by varying the quantity of hot air in the balloon.

Wooden block floating on water: the weight of an equal volume of water is greater than the weight of the block. By the principle of floatation a body floats if its displaced water equals the weight of the body when it is partially or completely immersed.

Ships and boats (Fig. 5.10a): designed on the principle of floatation, they carry passengers and goods over water; a ship would sink if its weight including the weight of passengers and goods became greater than the upthrust of water. (Brain Teaser: why does a ship of heavy steel float while a small rock sinks? Its hollow hull displaces a weight of water equal to its own weight before it is fully immersed.)

Submarine (Fig. 5.10b): it travels over as well as under water by the same principle. It floats when the weight of water equal to its volume is greater than its weight, remaining partially above the water level like a ship. It has tanks which can be filled with and emptied of seawater; when the tanks are filled the weight of the submarine increases, and as soon as its weight exceeds the upthrust it dives and remains under water; to come up the tanks are emptied.

blocks.title: Example 5.3
blocks.text: An empty meteorological balloon weighs 80 N and is filled with 10 cubic metres of hydrogen. How much can the balloon lift besides its own weight? Density of hydrogen 0.09 kg m^-3, density of air 1.3 kg m^-3. Solution: w = 80 N, V = 10 m^3, rho1 = 0.09 kg m^-3, rho2 = 1.3 kg m^-3. Upthrust F = weight of air displaced = rho2 g V = 1.3 kg m^-3 x 9.8 m s^-2 x 10 m^3 = 127.4 N. Weight of hydrogen w1 = rho1 V g = 0.09 kg m^-3 x 10 m^3 x 9.8 m s^-2 = 8.82 N. Total weight lifted F = w + w1 + w2; to lift the contents the total weight must not exceed F: 80 N + 8.82 N + w2 = 127.4 N, or w2 = 38 N.
